utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read the affirmation aloud that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit. Mr. Popovic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dosan, before I start putting questions to you, I would kindly ask you the following: Given that we use the same language, please listen carefully to my questions, pause shortly, and then answer in order for the interpreters to do their job properly. Also try to speak slowly also for the sake of the interpreters. Could you please state your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Milos Dosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of February, 1949, in Bistrica, Zepce municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you already testified before this Tribunal in the case against Mr. Milosevic on the 19th, 20th, 25th, 26th, and 31st of October, 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: During the proofing for your testimony today, did you have occasion to reread everything you had stated in your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If I would put to you the same questions today, would you still provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender Mr. Dosan's testimony transcript, which is at 65 ter 1662. We also have a version under seal, D011-2350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript under seal first will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00683 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00684.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will read out Mr. Dosan's testimony summary. During the period in question between the 15th of July, 1998, and until the end of the war in 1999, the witness commanded the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of the anti-aircraft Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia. At the same time, he commanded the garrison in Djakovica. In his testimony, the witness will explain what responsibilities he held and exercised as the brigade commander and which of those pertain to his capacity as the garrison commander in 1989 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As well as his participation at such meetings which were held in order to secure a proper functioning of the town of Djakovica. Those meetings were held together with representatives of the MUP and civilian authorities. The witness will explain the disposition and engagement as well as tasks of his unit in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. He will address the issue of the area of responsibility of his unit, the weapons they had at their disposal, and the fact that his unit was engaged in anti-aircraft defence of Kosovo and Metohija. He will testify about his contacts with the OSCE verifiers and weapons inspections carried out by the verifiers in his unit. The witness will also speak about the acts of terrorism on the part of the KLA in 1998 and 1999, and almost daily attacks of those terrorist forces, especially in those villages along the road between Djakovica and Decani, as well as in Djakovica itself. He will provide further explanation of specific tasks, goals, and engagements of his brigade in the defence of the country during 1999. The witness will confirm that his unit had never been assigned any tasks which would have required them to expel the civilian population and he never implemented such tasks. He will testify by the activities of his unit on the taking care, providing shelter, as well as providing population to the civilian population. The witness will also explain the measures which were undertaken in order to meet all necessary obligations under the laws of war and international humanitarian law as well as those measures taken against members of the Army of Yugoslavia who breached those rules. The witness will mention the 24th of March as the first day of bombardment, which is also the date stated in the indictment, and the event of the Djakovica mosque and library being hit. He will also address April 1999 and the fact that he had no knowledge about any events in the settlement of Cerim and that there was no indicia of any VJ members taking part in those crimes, and also there was no indicia of any MUP members. The witness will mention the 14th of April, 1999, and the massacre which happened as the refugee column was moving towards Meja when it was hit by NATO aviation. He will mention the 21st of April and the number of casualties among civilians in the refugee camp caused by NATO aviation. The witness will mention the events of the 27th and 28th of April, 1999. Those dates are stated in the indictment as the days of operations undertaken in Korenica and Meja. He will state that a part of his unit was engaged there exclusively along the blockade line in order to prevent KLA terrorists to approach the town of Djakovica, and that upon the unit's return, he was informed that they had no previous contact with any terrorists. He will confirm that he had not received any kind of information or report of any crimes being committed during that operation. The witness during his testimony will comment upon the statement of Nike Peraj and point out the obvious inaccuracies and untruths which that witness mentioned in his statement. Given that he was deployed in Djakovica, the witness can testify about events during the relevant period of time in that town including those events directly related to the NATO air campaign. Your Honours, this concludes the summary of testimony of Mr. Dosan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, before you continue, I'm concerned that what you may have in mind will have the same effect as we noticed with previous witnesses. You have tendered, pursuant to leave, the evidence of this witness in the form of a very extensive transcript. You now from your summary, and from what I see as the amended time that you expect to lead evidence in chief from this witness, would plan to lead him fairly meticulously through virtually everything. The point of transcript or statement evidence is that it lessens the need for a detailed examination-in-chief, the examination-in-chief merely to deal with any highlight or significant points, or to correct some confusion or error. Now, it's now moving into the fourth week of Defence evidence and we've drawn attention to this last week, we do it again now. It's not a sensible use of our time to have the witness spend hours, you estimate over four, going through again a large amount of material that is already admitted in the transcript. We certainly give the Defence a very free hand, but we must ask that there be a greater discipline in your time so that we are only dealing with any highlights and points of special significance in the examination-in-chief where the witness -- the main evidence of the witness is received in the form of previous transcript or of statement. If you would please bear that in mind with this witness and with future witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In any case, Defence will bear this in mind. At the beginning of my presentation today, I stated that the witness was -- the witness testified for five days in the Milosevic case. In any case, we won't come even close. We'll use far less time. We will question this witness in a different manner than he was in the Milosevic case, and there will be a number of documents that we will use during his testimony that we will try to use to explain things to the Court. We hope you will have an understanding for that, and we will try to meet your instruction in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dosan, were you ever a member of the VJ, and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the VJ as of the 12th of September, 1970, until the 31st of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 31st of December, 2001, were you pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What rank did you hold at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, briefly, can you explain to us at what positions you were within the VJ and previously JNA during your career?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. I was platoon commander, battery commander, artillery battalion commander, rocket regiment battalion commander, anti-aircraft defence brigade commander, inspector for rocket units with the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, chief of the commission for the control of implementation of the arms control protocol under Security Council Resolution 1244.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last position as the interpreter missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I was chief of the inspection or better to say commission, which was in charge of controlling the implementation of arms control under Resolution 1244 of the Security Council. And after that, chief of the inspection of military draft service in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us precisely what duties you performed in the VJ in 1989 and -- 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: In the first half of 1998 I was inspector for rocket units at the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. In the second part of 1998 and the first half of 1999, I was commander of the anti-aircraft defence brigade, the 52nd Artillery Rocket Anti-Aircraft Defence Brigade in Djakovica, and also the commander of the Djakovica garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the commander of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade, what were your basic duties and competencies within the brigade when you arrived there in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: The task of the anti-aircraft defence brigade was to engage any enemy targets in our air-space. That was my basic task as commander as well as the basic task of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you commanded the brigade as well as the garrison at the same time. Can you explain the difference between these two duties or roles you performed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. The basic function of mine was brigade commander. As for my duty as the garrison commander, that was an auxiliary duty in relation to the brigade duty. It came on top of my regular duties within the brigade. The duty of the brigade commander includes efficient use of the brigade, inflicting losses on the enemy in the air-space with minimum casualties in the unit, materiel, and personnel. The role of the garrison commander included providing order -- securing order and discipline in the garrison and securing proper functioning of life and work in the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly only, can you tell us whether there was a difference in the way you performed or one would perform these duties in peacetime and later on in war-time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As a rule theoretically, and that role should have been the same as well as the tasks. However, given that the war-time circumstances were changed, such roles entailed different duties to those in peacetime. There were certain differences in the way the garrison commander acts in peacetime and in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us, what was the situation like in the town of Djakovica and the surrounding area during 1998, or more specifically, in July when you arrived in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I arrived in Djakovica in the first half of July. This is what the situation was like. As for the four roads that lead from Pristina to Djakovica, three were totally blocked. That is to say that Metohija was almost completely cut off from Kosovo. I came along the only accessible road at that point in time, which was the longest one as well. However, security had to be provided there as well. That is to say, I arrived in a military convoy that had to be guarded due to constant attacks by the Siptar terrorist forces. As for the situation in the town of Djakovica, the unit that I came to command had already sustained losses. A senior sergeant from the medical corps had already been abducted and a soldier had already been killed. The situation was rather difficult, and it was reflected primarily in the very few supplies that reached the population because the town had been cut off as such. So all the goods that were needed for normal life were barely there. As for freedom of movement, there was hardly any. People, or rather, women and children, basically stood in queues in front of shops. Men went out only when pensions were being paid out because they received pensions and other social welfare payments were distributed regularly, and no one else could pick them up on anyone's behalf, so that is what the situation was when I arrived in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you speak of the freedom of movement, what were the reasons for that freedom of movement to be the way you described it just now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, it can be described in the following way: Women moved about town, whereas the men did not usually appear in the streets. Most of them were part of the terrorist units of the KLA, and those who were not were, I assume, afraid that they might be mobilised or so they may have been afraid because of the propaganda that was heard, so quite simply they did not appear in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just by way of clarification, when you speak of fear of mobilisation, fear of being mobilised by who?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: By the terrorists. They broke into villages or people's homes in town and they forcibly mobilised military-aged men. And they even sold weapons to them. That is to say that people had to buy their own rifles and then join various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us, did your unit take part in operations in the field in 1998 after you arrived in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. However, these were not really operations. Operations are a broad concept involving large units. These were are individual actions that were there by way of support for other units, so it was always military units upon orders from the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So what was the role of your unit in these operations, or rather, actions, I beg your pardon, and what was your attitude as brigade commander towards the part of the unit that took part in these actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, parts of my unit were sent to units that carried out actions on the basis of orders issued by the corps command or the forward command post of the command that was in Djakovica. From that moment onwards, my unit was commanded by the person who was in charge of the action. So until my troops returned to their original unit, they were not under my own command.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. During 1998, as garrison commander, did you have meetings with the representatives of the civilian authorities and the Ministry of the Interior in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that the civilian authorities functioned normally. There was a president of the municipality and there was the Municipal Assembly, and all organs of government functioned normally. From time to time, in order to resolve some specific matters, I would meet with the president of the municipality of Djakovica and with the chief of SUP of Djakovica. So it wasn't regularly, it was only from time to time, and only in order to handle specific matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So what was discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: At these meetings we would discuss problems, if there were any, in town. I remember, for instance, when there was a problem with Radonjic hydro system, when the water-supply of the town of Djakovica was brought into question. We had reservists in our units who had been mobilised and we discharged them so that the problem could be resolved. Also, when we were supposed to get the bakery working because the Siptars had withdrawn from all positions in town, all duties in town rather, in order to ensure normal food supplies, we singled out from our units people who had worked in bakeries previously and seconded them to work in the bakery in town. So that's the kind of problem that we tried to work out.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So were these problems that affected all the inhabitants of Djakovica at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Of course. All of the problems were common problems. The town -- the life in the town of Djakovica was the same for everyone, all civilians and all military men, all ethnicities, we all shared the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that during July and August 1998, a large number of people from surrounding villages came to Djakovica as internally displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that since I came in the month of June. However, it is possible that there were certain movements, but I have no direct knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the transcript, you arrived when in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: On the 9th of July, and I assumed my duty on the 15th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to speed things up, I'm now going to move on to the latter half of 1998, and I'd like to ask you whether you know that in October 1998 an agreement had been reached that envisaged the return of VJ units into barracks, and I'm also going to ask you whether you acted in accordance with that agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the agreement, and we received orders to act according to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you something. When I put my question to you, would you please pause for a moment and then start answering.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about October 1998 and all the way up to the end of 1998. Was there an increase in the number of members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No, there weren't any increases.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, General, that in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija towards the end of 1998 there was a mission of verifiers of the OSCE that was deployed there, and did you have any contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, my first contact with them was very sad. Dejan Arizanovic one of my soldiers, got killed on the 13th of November, 1998 in the Dulje canyon, the verifiers were 200 metres away from there. The situation was a very unpleasant one. He got killed when one of our food convoys was attacked. On that occasion, five of my soldiers were wounded. At the very entrance into the canyon, they came across the verifiers who were perhaps 2- or 300 metres away only.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In general terms, do you know what the task was of the OSCE Mission in the area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. I know their role and task was to monitor the implementation of the provisions of the said agreement, or rather, to monitor the cease-fire. Also, the withdrawal of units of the Army of Yugoslavia into barracks, the grouping of heavy weaponry in barracks as well. However, they were also responsible for security, or rather, they were supposed to guarantee that there would be no attacks during the cease-fire against the military, the police, civilians, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the members of the Verification Mission come to see you as brigade commander in Djakovica, and did they carry out any checks?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, the verifiers came to my unit. That was on the 16th of December, 1998. I met them; I spoke to them; they checked the weaponry there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, what type of weapons did they check?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Only launching mechanisms, and rocket systems called Strela 2m.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the mechanisms and the Strela 2m that they were checking?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: These are weapons for anti-aircraft defence. That is to say, it is launched from hand-held launchers, and it is used for targeting aircraft only up to an altitude of 3- to 4.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could such weapons be used in any way against targets on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No, not in a single case. Quite simply it cannot be used for any targets on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that my question became your answer here, so -- ah-hah, I see it's been fixed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, at that moment did the members of the KLA have aircraft or helicopters for which they needed to check this kind of anti-aircraft weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As far as I know at that point in time the KLA had no aircraft or helicopters or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So do you know what the reason was for checking such weaponry in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: It is very simple to conclude why, what was known and planned at the time was the NATO aggression. It was already then that they were planning to use the air force. Why else would be checking on such weapons? Actually, they were only counting the type of weapons that could be used in certain situations against an enemy air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we are on the subject of weapons, General, in your brigade did you have 30-millimetre anti-aircraft guns in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, in every one of the artillery battalions there was one battery respectably of anti-aircraft guns of 30-millimetre calibre. They were popularly known as Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the general continues answering these question, I would like to suggest that we see D011-3070 on our screens. Of course, only if our colleagues from the Prosecution do not mind because this document is not on the Defence 65 ter list. However, we did mention it in our notification as a document that we might use and that is a document that speaks of 30-millimetre anti-aircraft guns and how they are maintained. This is something that our witness could comment upon briefly. We would just like to use the document only two pages of it, rather, if our colleagues don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are going to deal with this very briefly. 3106 in B/C/S, please, could I have that page. Right now we do not have a translation into English of this page. It was sent for translation. It is being translated now. It's just one sentence in paragraph 85 that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "The anti-aircraft gun 30/2 millimetres is placed on an armoured vehicle. It is intended for targeting targets in the air, and if necessary, targets on the ground and in water." General, is this the way you understand it too?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is written there, yes, in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us briefly look at D011-3234 in the B/C/S version. And D011-3279 in the English version. Before that I am just going to ask if the witness could be given the binder that the Defence had already prepared for his use, of course with the permission of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you can see it on your screen so let us not waste any time, 439 is the paragraph that I'm looking at. "To defend firing positions, the 30/2 millimetre anti-aircraft gun can be used to target stationary and mobile targets on the ground and if necessary, targets on water." Very briefly, is that the rule that applies to 30-millimetres guns like the one that you had within your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is the rule. And it is still in force. It hasn't been changed. So it is fully in force, and yes, that is the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. A few questions about the weapon itself, but before that I seek to tender this document, or rather, we should perhaps have it marked for identification given that we are still awaiting translation of the pages I have just shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00686 marked for identification. And if I could, Your Honours, correct the numbers given previously at page 2, line 20 and line 23, instead of D00683 under seal, the number should have been D00684 under seal, and respectively instead of D00684, it should have been D00685. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, did the verifiers ask you about this weapon system in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No. They were not interested at all in this type of weapon. They never inquired about it, and they never asked to see such guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We saw in the rule that it can also be used against ground targets. In which situations could it be put to such use, in particular in relation to other type of guns and cannons of large calibre, what are its shortcomings and good sides?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As stated here, this weapon can also be used against fortified ground, and if necessary water targets. And in that sense, the weapon was used. Whenever my unit received a task to take part in an action, it always had a Praga or a BOV 20/3 millimetres in order to provide support to the unit. It usually happened when we expected to come across fortified targets such as bunkers and fortifications used by terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This weapon in relation to, say, 60 and 82 millimetre mortars as well as other guns and cannons such as recoilless guns, how does it behave, or would such a weapon used against ground targets amount to excessive force?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No. We used this weapon to prevent that especially so that there is no excessive force. This is a precise mechanism, and it does not have the usual dispersion or margin of error that one usually has with other artillery pieces. Given that it's of a lesser calibre, it causes less destruction than other means used to support units or to destroy fortified positions. It is precisely for that reason why we used this type of weapon in order to cause as little destruction as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that some parts of your unit took part in certain actions, and we are still in 1998, perhaps you can explain to us what was the nature of such actions? Were they offensive or defensive?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Those actions were undertaken exclusively to protect our units and to open up communications and roads. Because the roads were blocked, our units, and especially our border units and border stations were in danger because they could not receive food, water, fuel, ammunition, and all other types of supply making up the logistics of a unit. It was only used then in such cases. Such actions always lasted shortly. They never lasted more than a single day, depending, of course, the number of terrorist forces and degree of fortification along certain routes. Unfortunately, this area was very difficult to navigate and difficult to defend because it is in a mountainous area on forbidden terrain, and there was no other way to provide supplies other than using certain mountain paths which, for the most part, were taken up or blocked by the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many such actions were there that your unit participated in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I think between two and four. Two to three or three to four.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, there is an event in Djakovica and its environs mentioned in the indictment. The Prosecution asserts that that event took place between the 24th of March and the 20th of May. Vlastimir Djordjevic is being charged with those events. Therefore, I will focus on them in particular as they occurred in 1999. First of all, during the state of war did you keep the war diary for your brigade yourself or anyone else whom you tasked with doing so?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, we kept the brigade war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in brief what were its contents, what type of events were recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: The war diary was something that our unit was obliged to keep as much as any other unit in war time. All important events are recorded that are of significance for the unit and reflect the situation in the unit. First and foremost, such events are entered that have a certain importance for the unit, such as losses, successes, tasks issued to the unit, manner of implementing those tasks and how they were implemented, the degree of participation of key officer personnel, and everything else that makes up the history of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have P5 -- 958 put on the screen. It is tab 2 in your binder. So P958. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Let me find it in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go immediately to page 4 in both versions. I think you have those in hard copy for your perusal. The date is the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: These are the pages. Let's look at entry number 9 and up to entry number 16, which is on the next page, but let's start with the first one. First of all, does this page of the diary have to do with the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that at 6.00 p.m. the -- there was an air-raid signalled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: At 8.00 in the evening there was an air-strike against ground targets?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We also see that the 2nd battery of the 1st SARD PVO opened fired from Cabrat on targets in the air-space. Where is Cabrat in relation to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Cabrat is a hill overlooking Djakovica town. The old part of Djakovica is at the very foot of the hill just above Katolicka Street and that is basically the centre of town, the old town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the air-raid was signalled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I was on Cabrat hill. Our unit was stationed there. We had our radars used to detect air-space targets. Cabrat hill is a very good feature at which one can place anti-aircraft defence and monitoring equipment. I was there in a shelter on top of Cabrat hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Chronologically speaking, you say here that at 2140 hours, there was a group of airplane which arrived from Italy towards the FRY, and then we see 2 hours 45 minutes; is that already on the 24th of March in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And next we have item 16, 930 hours air-raid alert sounded. Are these the events you recorded in your diary for the 24th and 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit D006-4300.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 3, General. This is the document. General, this is sent to the commission for co-operation with the ICTY expert team. Your name is there as well as your address. The date is the 28th November, 2009 [as interpreted] concerning unit engagements on the 24th of March, 1999. Statement. Who did you give this statement to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I provided this statement to the commission for co-operation with the ICTY to their so-called expert team. They asked me to provide that statement after a book was published by the foundation for humanitarian law and assistance. In that book Djakovica is mentioned. Given that by that time I had already retired, they called me in and asked me to provide a statement about a particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you provide your opinion, your view of the event. On the 24th of March, were there any NATO aviation air-strikes in Djakovica itself and its environs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, in the town of Djakovica itself as well as against the barracks in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last paragraph of the first page you say that the -- it says as follows: "I was on Cabrat hill when the NATO planes carried out their first strikes. I was there together with the troops from the command battalions." Is this what you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was on Cabrat hill when we saw the first sorties and strikes. With me there was the command battalion staff following the situation. From that feature, I could hear the results of those strikes, although from the shelter itself I could not see where the ordnance had landed. Although I could hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: There you say in the first paragraph: "When I came out of the shelter, I could see the results of detonations on Katolicka Street, and I could hear fire engines. Given that I didn't see the strikes, I could only presume what had happened in Katolicka Street, and I believe it was a result of the strikes of NATO airplanes." Could you tell us exactly what did you see, hear, observe?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. After the initial explosions I came out of the shelter. Give than my position was above Katolicka Street, I could see that it was on fire. It had beautiful small old buildings and houses. There were beautiful old buildings made of wood and attached to each other. It was practically impossible to stop the spreading of fire. I could see from the hill that the street was ablaze, and I could hear the fire engines coming in and trying to put out fires. That's what I could see the first night. After several days, I passed along that part of town as our barracks Devet Jugovica that was our basic barracks and was very close by. It was practically situated in the continuation of Katolicka Street. It was also targeted and mostly destroyed. So when I got there, I could see the extent of the destruction in Katolicka Street, and it was really in a poor state. It was a pity to see what that looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you have any information concerning what caused the fire in Katolicka Street on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I don't have any direct knowledge. I could not see it from the hill. However, Major Zlatko Odak who was my subordinate officer and who was deployed in Devet Jugovica barracks, because this was a logistical unit, he claimed that he could see a missile fall in that part of town. He also said that this was what caused the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you were on Cabrat hill, could you hear or see what part of town was targeted by the NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: On the first night, and there were air-strikes on Djakovica every day, but on the first night I could hear three explosions. I could not see where the rockets fell, but I did see the street which was ablaze and later on I heard that the Devet Jugovica barracks was also hit on that occasion, so was a police facility situated within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of your statement you say: "I claim that my units and myself personally have nothing to do with the alleged destruction of this part of Djakovica and the said religious facility. I have no information that other units or parts of forces of Serbia or FRY took part in purposeful destruction of the town." And you say that these facilities were destroyed during the NATO air-strikes on civilian and military facilities in Djakovica town. Is that what you saw on that occasion and what you say today when you are talking about these events?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I fully confirm that and I can reiterate the same claim. Neither myself nor my unit nor any other part of Serbian or FRY forces participated in this crime in any way whatsoever. And it was a crime. I claim that the fire was caused by NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I propose to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00687.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see D006-4304.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 4 in your binder, General. General, we can see your order. It says, Command of the 52nd ARBR PVO. The 24th of March, 1999. The title is, taking Measures in the Events of a Bombing, and I would ask if we could please see the next page in both versions. Under item 4, General, and then under the second dash after the initial attacks, commanders command priorities will be preventing panic, desertion, and criminal activities. Can you please clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, most of my soldiers, including myself, had experience with NATO air-strikes for the first time, so naturally it was to be expected that panic would spread among the members of the unit, that it would be much more difficult to command, and that incidents could occur which would not be good for the situation within the unit. That was why, in timely fashion, I wrote orders and sent them to all my subordinate officers and commanders of other units instructing them how to act in such a situation. Considering that after combat operations there are many consequences that are out of control, I strictly prohibited any violation of humanitarian law. Strikes against the town regularly caused fire, window panes bursting, doors being broken, and as a consequence of that there were lots of goods that were in the street. I made sure that in such a situation when panic was spreading, there would be no looting or any other incidents of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your position throughout the NATO bombing campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: That was the position of my corps commander, my own position, and the position of all my colleagues who were in Kosovo and Metohija. That was the way that we were taught, that we were brought up, that we had to stick to our soldierly honour and our officer's honour, and that we had to keep it always and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you please have a look at item 9. Let me not read out the entire paragraph. Does this relate to what you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, just read it for yourself and then please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This is just what I said. Officers, commanding units, but also all their subordinates have to show that they are able to fight for the freedom of their homeland in every situation, and they always have to behave honourably as soldiers considering that in our people a soldier was always equated with honour and honesty. I insisted on this in order to ensure that these moral qualities would not be soiled in any way or jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The exhibit will be received. It's been pointed out to me that the translation into English has the date of the 26th of March whereas the original seems to be the 24th. The other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, it's quite possible because the date on the Serbian version of the document is the 26th of March, but let me check. Yes, you are quite right. The translation says the 24th. It should be but let me check with general.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, what does the heading of the document say, what is the date of the document that we just commented on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I'm writing [as interpreted] it just now. It says here the 26th of March, 1999. That was the second day after the break-out of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be Exhibit D00688.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now return to the document P958. And look at page 8 in the B/C/S version. I'm sorry, it's page 11. It's the 31st of March, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 31st of March, 1999, General. That's right. It's item 2.3 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 31st of March, 1999, and in your diary, you say that a radar was hit and that the following soldiers were killed on that occasion, Djordje Cimbaljevic and Zoran Ivanovic. When I say you wrote that in the diary I didn't mean you personally, but the unit whose commander you were. If we turn the page to the 1st of April, 1999 you also mention here something relating to soldier Cimbaljevic and Ivanovic. Can you please just have a look at that. I'm not asking you for any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now if we could please see Exhibit D006-4309.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your diary, you did not record any unusual incidents on the 31st of March and the 1st of April. We can see here once again this is addressed to the commission for co-operation with the ICTY to the expert team unit activities on the 1st of April, 1999, your statement Milos Dosan. What is this about? Did you give another statement, and if you did, what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I recently explained, this is the same commission to which I gave the previous statement. All events relating to Djakovica mentioned in the said book were something that I was supposed to comment for this commission. I was to describe to the best of my recollection, as I had no documents, what happened on the said days and in connection with the said event described in the said book. And so I gave this statement to the said commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you were asked questions about events which took place in the Cerim settlement. Could we please see the next page of this version of your statement where you say: "I myself travelled by the route sited and once again I observed no activities in the Cerim quarter which is in the immediate vicinity of the location where our soldiers were killed. According to statement by the 3rd Battalion commander, Major Dusko Vukasinovic, one of whose platoons was located in the Vinarski Podrum facility in the immediate vicinity of the Cerim quarter, they did not report that they had observed any kind of activities which might prompt any actions by the VJ or the police." Can you please briefly clarify what you stated here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I described here the events which were related with the deaths of my soldiers because the location where they were killed at the radar, it's a place called Lum-Bunar, and it is close to the Cerim quarter. On the previous night when we were extinguishing the fires and pulling out our soldiers, I passed through this quarter. It could have been about 2.00 a.m., and I observed nothing. There was no electricity in the town of Djakovica at the time, so everything looked spooky at night. It was very difficult and dangerous to move around. I had one of my units in a facility which is called Vinarski Podrum, which is maybe 3 or 400 metres away as the crow flies from the said Cerim quarter. The commander of this unit informed me that his soldiers and officers who were stationed there, as our soldiers were never without any officers, informed me that they had not observed any activities or events in that part of town. For that reason, I have no information about what is mentioned in the humanitarian law centre's book, and on the basis of that, I expressed the claim that neither myself nor anyone else from my unit had anything to do with the said crime committed in the Cerim quarter. We are also not aware of who might have been the perpetrator of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, my question for you was whether at that moment you had any information whatsoever that any sort of crime had been committed in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see here that you are discussing the 31st of March and the 1st of April. If someone were to ask you about what was happening during the night between the 1st and the 2nd of April, would that change anything in your testimony, or did you have any information about any crimes committed during that night between April 1st and 2nd?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No, nothing would be different because the said soldiers spent about one month in this Vinarski Podrum facility. I did visit them on the previous night, but the soldiers were quartered there in this facility throughout the whole time. They were not in the barracks, and I still claim, as does the commander of the said unit, that we did not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, what was the situation in Djakovica like at the time? Were there already any consequences of the NATO air-strikes against military and civilian facilities in the town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As I said, there were air-strikes against the town every day. There were already many facilities that were destroyed, many shop windows had been destroyed as a consequence of detonations of bombs, buildings had been set ablaze, some houses had been destroyed, some military facilities were destroyed, but so were some civilian facilities. Gas stations had been targeted, and there was practically not a single one left in tact. There were air-strikes against the town of Djakovica all the time including the town itself and also its immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have talked about Katolicka Street and how the old houses had been built and what were the consequences that one single rocket may have caused. What were the effects of NATO bombs on other parts of the town?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As I was in the town of Djakovica for the most part of this period, I can say that they used particular types of ordnance for particular targets. I was watching when a gas station called Stella was hit. At the moment when it was hit, the reservoirs which were underground started flying across town as tin cans. Actually, I did not see this, but I went to see later on how a tobacco-producing facility called Virginia, which had five levels, was burst by a bomb from the roof to the ground even though there were thick concrete slabs between each floor. They were almost half a metre thick. They were using various kinds of ordnance and the attacks on anti-aircraft units were mostly guided missiles. When they targeted facilities, they also used cruising missiles, which have very great destructive power, but also bombs that were smaller, bigger. They also used cluster bombs, special kinds of bombs that would use the electricity to fail. So they used all kinds of ordnances that they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we take the break, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D006-4313 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 6 in your binder, General. We see your order dated the 2nd of April, 1999. Again, I don't want to read out the entire order. It speaks of international humanitarian law and the observance thereof. Could you just give us your brief comments with regard to the entire document, notably 2, 3, and 4, and tell us what you insisted upon here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. That is my order, and I hereby order that on all occasions and at all points in time, the provisions of international humanitarian law should strictly be adhered to, that all units should abide by international humanitarian law, and also that it is their duty to provide information if they find out that someone is not complying with international humanitarian law. I state here that all possible perpetrators will be punished. That is to say, if anyone commits anything that is in contravention of international humanitarian law. I also provide instructions to security organs who in such a situation would hand the perpetrators over to military courts. Also, I state here that all members of the brigade should be made aware of this order. I particularly make it incumbent upon commanders of subordinate units to bear this in mind on all occasions and to take measures to prevent any form of non-compliance with international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were there any documents that every member of the Army of Yugoslavia had that instructed them to abide by international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Of course. All members of the unit, starting from myself all the way to the very last member of the brigade, had instructions accompanied by specific excerpts and descriptions of situation that anyone may face in a situation of war. This was pocket-sized. It was laminated in plastic so it could remain undamaged even if one's uniform got wet, for instance. So it could not be destroyed under any circumstances basically. Therefore, no one could say that they were not aware of international humanitarian law and how it was to be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00690, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-4315.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's number 7 in your binder, General. So we see this is a commander -- this is a document of the command of the 52nd Brigade dated the 6th of April, 1999. Paragraph 1 says: "Forces under the brigade command and deployment of engagement." And number 2 says: "Attached and resubordinated units." Could you please explain to us what paragraphs 1 and 2 mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Of course. In this survey, we see the forces that were under the direct command of the brigade and that were deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Popovic's microphone please be switched off, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, it says, for instance that the 1st Battalion Skivljane, and then the 1st Rocket Battalion the 3rd Artillery Battalion at the Mitar Vujinovic border post sector, so these were units that were under my command only, and it is our officers from our brigade that commanded those units. The second part, the second paragraph pertains to units that had been attached and resubordinated to other units by way of support for particular activities. In actual fact, every unit had the duty of protecting itself from air-strikes. These units that were attached and resubordinated to other units were deployed with the intention of reinforcing those other units in an anti-aircraft sense because these other units had not been trained and equipped to target aircraft and the like, so this is what this survey shows. For instance, it says that one battery from the 3rd Artillery Battalion was in the area of Zub, then another one was somewhere in the command of the Pristina Corps area, then the 549th Motorised Brigade, so whenever necessary they were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, tell me, under whose command were these attached and resubordinated units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, the very word "resubordination" means that they were commanded by the commanding officer of the unit to which that part of my brigade was attached or resubordinated, namely, that unit was used only on the basis of orders issued by the commanding officer of the unit to which that part of my unit had been attached and they acted upon his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00691.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, since we are talking about the 6th of April and the period after that, could you tell me whether there was a major offensive by the terrorist forces in that period of time in the area of Morina and Kosare facing the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, on the 7th of April, in the area of the Kosare border post, there was a large influx of terrorist forces from the Republic of Albania that were supported by large calibre artillery from the army of the Republic of Albania. At the same time, they had fire support from the NATO air force. One of my soldiers got killed in that attack. His name was Nikola Popovic. Lieutenant Misic was also wounded. I'm talking about my own unit, but this was an attack in a wide area and there was a serious danger, namely, that they take particular elevations, certain parts of our country, that is. Also, this intimated an almost certain second stage of the aggression, that is to say land invasion. The aggression started on the 24th of March in the air but by then there was the looming danger of ground attacks, which this was in actual fact. It was aggression on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D006-4318 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 8 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't appear to have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-4318. That's the number that I have. We just need a second to check this. In the meantime, I'm going to move on to the next document and then we'll go back to this one once we've checked what this is all about. So could we now please have D006-4320.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 9 in your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have this document? That seems to be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your order dated the 10th of April, 1999. In paragraph 1, you speak of the use of inhumane combat resources. Could you please read this and tell us what it is that you meant and what is your knowledge of the use of such equipment in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is my order regulating that particular matter and this is what I say in paragraph 1: "Unit commanders shall undertake all necessary measures to protect units, both on march and during relocation as well as in combat engagement sectors, both from enemy aircraft operating from air-space and from the use of the latest ordnance, including inhumane ones." During the NATO aggression, we kept relocating all the time. Units had to be relocated all the time because they faced the danger of being destroyed if they were to spend any longer amount of time in a particular area. That is why I make this order. Especially because by then, these inhumane ordnance was already being used. I'm primarily referring to cluster bombs, but also ammunition containing depleted uranium. You can see that this is an order dated the 10th of April, that is to say that immediately after this attempt was made to carry out an aggression on land, NATO air-strikes were intensified involving the use of all possible resources in order to support the influx of terrorists from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we briefly deal with paragraph 4 of this order, unarmed persons, women, children, and the elderly and others that happen to be in the unit combat deployment sector should be treated humanely and on the basis of principles of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: But of course. Throughout I issued such orders, but also my corps commander issued such orders to me as well, namely to observe the provisions of international humanitarian law all the time invariably, and there is practically not a single order where we did not refer to that as well, where we did not caution the troops about that. Inter alia, because units kept changing, new soldiers, new officers were being brought in so there was no such order or suggestion that was superfluous. I believe that they were supposed to be part and parcel of every order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00692, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have been advised that things are fine now with the previous document and that we can now have it on the screen. It is D006-4318, which is your tab number 8, General. That's the document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is another order of yours dated 10th of April, 1999, where in item 1 you say that all perpetrators of criminal offences shall be immediately escorted to a competent investigating judge of the Pristina Corps Command military court, accompanied by a criminal report. In item 2 you say that the measures specified in item 1 of this order shall also be taken against conscripts and volunteers in the military. And item 3, you speak of briefing the entire force and all the units on all measures taken. Could you please comment briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This is in the spirit of the rest of my decisions and orders. I hereby order that criminal reports should be made and that all perpetrators should be brought before an investigating judge on the Pristina Corps Command military court. I also ordered the chief of security including the military police, which is authorised to arrest unit members in case of certain crimes, that they should do so without any hesitation. As for item 2, I made it clear that the same applied to any conscripts and volunteers. I also ordered that reports should be submitted to the command on the measures taken, but also to inform all other units so as to act preventively. Say there was an individual case of violation of international humanitarian law in a unit, I ordered by virtue of this order, that other units be informed of that through our security service so that attention should be drawn to the importance of preventing similar occurrences in other units and that this should be done by the commanders responsible. I also stated that unit commanders shall be held responsible for the implementation of this order, and I in turn answered to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00693.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I would ask for D006-4333.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 10. This is another order of the 10th of April, 1999. It concerns the Pristina Corps Command and the undertaking of measures to defend the FRY order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, have a look at item 6, please. This is --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, I believe this may be a wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D006-4333. Sorry, it is actually D006-4323. 4333 will be the next document. Yes. It says Pristina Corps Command. That is the correct document. Could we please go to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, have a look at item 6. I would like you to comment briefly. What is it that the Pristina Corps Command is ordering here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, this came from the commander of the Pristina Corps to all subordinate commanders and units. He insists on the improvement of discipline and soldierly appearance and ordering us to prevent any misconduct by individuals, looting, murder, et cetera, whilst upholding the reputation of the army by virtue of our own conduct. Our commanders, in particular General Lazarevic who was my commander, ordered what I ordered to my subordinates. We always insisted on order, discipline, honourable conduct, and the avoidance of unnecessary use of force. We insisted on all the virtues of an army which is fighting not only for its existence, but its reputation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'd like to ask you to look at item 15, para 2. It says: "Make an analysis of -- make an analysis of the response of R/S." First of all, tell us whether there were any reservists in your unit, by what means they arrived there and how, following what documents, and how were they allocated to different units? This is a complex question but it covers, I believe, all the necessary aspects we need to know about reservists and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: To tell you right away, I had volunteers in my unit. I believe we need to define the term "volunteer" first.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The question I asked did not have to do with reservists, but only with volunteers, so volunteers only.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. Volunteers are people, military conscripts, who had not received call-up papers. They had not been mobilised, but guarded by their patriotic feelings, they reported to units of the Army of Yugoslavia. Specifically, in my unit I had a number of volunteers. They arrived from the command of the Pristina Corps. They were always brought in by an officer. These were not individuals or groups who came by themselves. They would always be accompanied by an officer from the corps command with their personnel cards and the necessary military documents from which we could conclude what their specialties were and military background. According to that, they were then allocated to certain units. Upon their arrival, we would take charge of them, we would issue them with weapons, and dispatch them according to their military specialty or branch specialty. For example, if they served the military term as radio men, they would be sent to our communications unit. If someone manned artillery pieces, they were then assigned to such units. If a person had been a nurse, then that person was sent to the field clinic. In any case, when we assigned those soldiers to different units irrespective of their numbers, they were never put in a single unit. As a rule, they could not comprise more than one-third of a unit, and they were always commanded by an establishment officer. It did happen that people arrived in the unit who, in our view, were unable to meet their obligations and duties. In particular, because our unit was an anti-aircraft unit where one needs to have good eyesight, one needs to be fit so that the unit could relocate frequently. Such volunteers who we could not use properly, were returned to the corps command and then they were assigned to other units. That is the answer. I did have volunteers in my unit. As of the moment when they joined the ranks, there were no exception. Internally we called them volunteers because they joined the unit honourably as opposed to others who, for example, fled the country when there was mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there certain rules in place concerning the number of volunteers which could be in a single unit, who could be in a single unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As I've just said, they could not have comprised more than one-third of a unit. For example, if there were 30 soldiers in a platoon, there could not have been more than 10 volunteers. The formula was precise. They never appeared as a majority group, and they were never commanded by a person who had escorted them to the unit. They were always commanded by our establishment active duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00694.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next could we see D006-4333.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is your tab 11. It is your order of the 13th of April, 1999. Please have a look at item 3, the sentence begins with: "Alcohol consumption and instances of defeatism, desertion, refusal or failure to obey orders are to be vigorously prevented. Greatest attention, care, and responsibility is to be exercised in matters involving personal appearance, treatment and conduct through troop reviews, and direct contact." Could you please comment briefly on this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I can tell you this, we persistently insisted on the maintaining of order and discipline. Alcohol is never a good thing, especially not in war time because people have weapons, ammunition, and they are constantly under stress. As for the second part where personal appearance is mentioned, in Djakovica, for example, when the post office was still working, people would come in from their border posts to call home and, of course, among them were those who did not have any soldierly appearance, they wore dirty uniforms, unshaven, and unkempt, which was due to the conditions under which they lived at the time. However, this did not amount to proper soldierly appearance. This was particularly announced among the reservists, as we called them. They were frequently somewhat older and who didn't look good in uniform anyhow, but in view of the circumstances and because of the fact that they had to spend prolonged periods of times along the line at Kosare were quite unkempt. As for the insignia, no other insignia was allow save for the insignia of the Army of Yugoslavia, and there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: While we are on the topic of insignia, can you tell us, do you have any kind of information that there were any members of paramilitary formations in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I spent most of the time in Djakovica but also I travelled frequently to other units of mine which were deployed all the way from Pec to Kijevo, Pristina, Gnjilane and further afield. I never saw paramilitary formations. The only paramilitary formation there was was the terrorist KLA. Although, I have to admit that I did not see a single member of the army. Based on the reports of my subordinate officers and my personal insight, I can say that I never saw any paramilitary formation members anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could it please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00695.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see Exhibit D006-2363.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And General that is your tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-2363. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report which your command sent to the Pristina Corps Command, and the date is the 14th of April, 1999. Under item 1, second paragraph, you say: "They did not attack features and units of the brigade, but they did attack refugee convoys in the immediate vicinity of the deployment sector of our units in the area of the village of Ripaj-Madanaj and the Terzijski bridge, which led to a massacre." General, do you remember this incident? Where did it take place and what did you directly learn about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the incident. I could almost say that I was an eye-witness. It happened in the Meja settlement when the NATO aircraft attacked a column of civilian refugees who were Albanians by ethnicity. Two aircraft attacked the column, and by order of the corps commander, I was sent to the spot to see what could be done. At the same time, I ordered the chief of the medical service to send an ambulance from our infirmary and see if any help could be provided to the people. I arrived there perhaps half an hour after the air-strike, and I can say that the scene was really horrible. The bodies were still smouldering. Parts of tractors and ox carts were thrown around. Some people had been burnt to death. Some were dismembered. The whole scene was horrible. What was characteristic was that at the head of the column was an elderly gentleman. He could have been around 75, and he was dapper. So I approached him and I asked him what had happened. He told me that there were two aircraft, that he had heard explosions, and there was nothing else that he could say. Now, this is what I find interesting. In Djakovica, we did not have any TV equipment or studio to able to record it. A TV crew had arrived from Prizren. I was with this gentleman all the time when the TV crew arrived. He suddenly changed, it was a real metamorphosis. He hunched his back, he looked like a poor devil, he began speaking in a warped Serbian, and when asked by the journalist what had happened, he said that something had exploded, that he did not know whether these had been aircraft or a shell or a bomb, and if they were aircraft, whose aircraft they were. So in my presence, an unbelievable change of his statement occurred. His behaviour also changed as if he had been trained for a different role. This is what I can say now, and I describe that in my book as well. But that is the truth. So we sent our team to the spot, very little could be done. Later on we received a report from the Djakovica hospital about how many people had perished, and we learned that they were mostly women and children. They were but few men. I have a feeling that the only man in the column was the elderly gentleman who was leading everyone else. That is my impression, and that is the truth as I saw it firsthand. I am not sure if I have managed to depict the scene to you, but it is certainly a scene that I would not like to remember often.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00696.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see Exhibit D006-4336.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 13, General. This is a regular combat report from your command sent to the Pristina Corps Command, dated 16th of April, 1999. Can you please focus on item 1, paragraph 3 says: "Between 750 and 810 hours on the 16th of April, the enemy dropped propaganda leaflets from aircraft in the entire brigade zone." Can you please explain what sort of incident this was, how frequent was it, and what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time that the leaflets were dropped on the 16th of April. If that had happened earlier, we would have reported that. They were dropped from aircraft in large quantities, and there was practically no spot where one could not find them.
