You could find them all over the town, but also blown by the wind, they would reach all places. The leaflets were produced on top quality paper, so even if they got wet because of dew or rain or if they were exposed to sun, they would still be in good shape. The contents were varied. One of the leaflets included a list of commanders whom they claimed they continually observed. Another one included invitation to soldiers to desert their units. They were also leaflets who could frighten anyone. Namely, the leaflets were dropped two or three days after the beginning of the bombing campaign with strategic B-52 bombers. It is well known that they can carry up to 20 tonnes of ordnance. One of the leaflets showed an image of this aircraft dropping carpet bombs, and the text said that they would be used in unlimited quantities until such a time when they managed to drive out the police and the military out of Kosovo. Of course, I saw these aircraft which were flying over my positions. They were at a very high altitude so that we couldn't shoot them down, but they looked like jumbo jets, and it was really scary to look at them, even when they were not bombing. There were other leaflets as well, but these were the most typical ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00697.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, now that we are discussing leaflets, could we please see Exhibit D006-2513, which is your tab 14, General. And you can see a leaflet. My question to you is whether you are familiar with this leaflet and its contents? Did you ever have an occasion to see this leaflet personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this leaflet, but it was not dropped from aircraft. Its form was that of a red sheet of paper with black lettering. Of course, I cannot read Albanian, but my officers translated it for me. Most of my officers in my unit, who are from Kosovo and Metohija, have a command of the Siptar language and they explained to me that this is a leaflet discussing the situation and addressed primarily, if not only to the Albanian, that is to say the Siptar population. The leaflet explains to them that the KLA cannot protect them and that it invites them and recommends to them to leave the territory of Kosovo and Metohija temporarily and directs them to certain axes. They are told to go to Albania and to Macedonia. And at the end it is said that they are invited to do so by the president of the republic, Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness said it wasn't dropped from aircraft but he hasn't told us exactly how he came across it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard what the presiding judge said, please tell us how you came into possession of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: We received certain instructions and orders ordering any member of the unit who would find any leaflets to hand them in to his superior. These leaflets were found across town, they were not dropped from aircraft, and an officer brought them to the command. I cannot remember who it was, but they were brought after having been found in the town of Djakovica. So they were not dropped from aircraft but one of the officers who was also stationed in the Djakovica town, I think it was one from the logistics battalion who found them and brought them to the command to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00698.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see Exhibit D006-4371, and that is your tab 15, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we can see here an order but it says at the top "Garrison Command." Securing the civilian population, that's the title, the date is the 17th of April, 1999, and under item 1 you say: "All units in the Djakovica garrison zone of responsibility shall take the measures necessary to care for the civilian population." General, please let me not read the rest of the paragraph to you, please read it for yourself and then tell us what were the measures that you took to provide care to the civilians, and what were the measures taken to do all the other things that you explain under item 1?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is my order in my capacity as garrison commander. There were orders that I issued as the brigade commander, and others that I issued as the garrison commander. As I said, my role as the garrison commander was to take care of the order and discipline in the town, to ensure that life functioned normally in the town for everyone, co-operate with the authorities, which were operating throughout this time, and also with the units of the MUP. I needed to help them to take care about the civilians and make the life easier as it was becoming more and more complicated every day. Primarily this was caused by the continuous bombing campaign, certain facilities had already been destroyed, and another reason was that the population was also exposed to the NATO attacks. Especially after the attack on the Siptar refugee column, there was a danger that by accident they might be targeted by NATO air force attacks because the aircraft flying at high altitudes could not always make a selection and determine who is who. Therefore, in co-ordination with the MUP organs and civilian authorities, we would occasionally meet in order to resolve specific issues. If it was needed to resolve the issue of water-supply or bread supply or electricity supply, then we from the military would release certain men from our units if they were, for example, mechanics or could help to repair certain equipment or if they were bakers, or anyone else who could prevent a possible catastrophe that might arise under such circumstances. So that was the purpose of this order. It further says that we have to know what are the numbers of the civilians and their movements and how well they are supplied at any given time so that we would be able to help them. In any case, these activities had humanitarian character, and we really had good intentions to make life easier for the people. At the same time we would make it easier for ourselves because we were also living in the same town.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would be interested in the following: Could you tell us specifically once again how often were meetings of the garrison command held, and also at these meetings, I am primarily referring to discussions with representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, did you discuss any actions on the ground or anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, we would meet only when absolutely necessary. Namely, these were not regular meetings. We would meet when the situation was such that something had to be done urgently in order to make it possible for the town to function. In this situation when we especially from the air defence were a constant target, even if we wanted to, we were unable to carry out long discussions. We would meet up to resolve a specific problem and then we would go our separate ways. We did not have any other discussions. We had no time for that. And also as far as security is concerned, a brigade commander and the chief of SUP and the president of the municipality would really be a highly desirable target for the NATO air force, the Siptar terrorists were in town, and they were always able detect our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give me a specific answer to the second part of my question. I think you've answered the first part, but my question was also whether in discussions with the representatives of the Ministry of the Interior at the meetings that you described just now when you had them and under the circumstances under which you had them, did you ever discuss land actions or anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No, no. We did not go into the subject of activities and tasks of others. I've already said we would meet very briefly, the meetings were very short, and we met only to resolve a specific problem in the garrison. I did not discuss with them our own actions or did I ask them about their actions. I had the feeling that the chief of SUP knew very little about these anti-terrorist actions, but I had no need to ask them about that. I had my own obligations within the brigade. When I met up with them, we resolved matters very quickly. Sometimes we would have very brief meetings as we stood, we would not even sit down for a meeting, we would simply deal with matters quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, these were primarily logistical problems that you discussed, logistics related to life in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: We only dealt with the problems that the local self-government or rather the municipality could not resolve on its own. I've already said that the organs of civilian government did function so it was only the problems that they could not resolve that we dealt with. It primarily had do with repairing the water-supply system, the electric system, et cetera. These people were in our units so no one else could relieve such a person of his duty. I was the only one who could do that, and it was usually at the initiative of the president of the municipality that we would resolve such matters. Whenever we could, we tried to meet their requirements and to resolve such problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago in your response you mentioned treatment of the civilian population. I would be interested in the following: From the beginning of the NATO bombing on the 24th of March onwards, did you notice any large-scale movements of the civilian population, and if so, what were the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: There were movements, and they coincided with the beginning of NATO air force activity. There were movements on a daily basis. These were groups numbering 200 to 300 persons, sometimes they were smaller -- well, the biggest group I saw was, say, 300, 350 people. I did not count them, but that is what I saw. They assembled -- they would assemble at a particular place and then they would move on, but there were movements of the population, yes. And may I add something else, the intensity of civilian movement somehow coincided with the increase in the activity of NATO air force. Of course, at first it was a bit less and then later on perhaps the largest population movements took place not on the first days of the NATO aggression but say after five, six, or ten days when the air force already started using bigger bombs, especially when people started talking about ammunition with depleted uranium. That's when there was more movement. And of course, they arrived in waves, as it were, hardly ever was it a single family that would move. They had areas where they would assemble and then they would move on. They moved on foot or on tractors or any other vehicles that they would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00699.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to ask for D006-4340.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is number 16 in your binder. We can see a criminal report dated the 17th of April, 1999. General, are you aware of this criminal report, and very briefly, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this criminal report. It is a criminal report against three of my soldiers from my own unit who tried to rape two Albanian women in the area of the village of Crmljanje the very moment I was informed about this, I sent the military police to arrest these men, and they handed them over immediately to the military prosecutor in Pristina. So that's the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00700.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, now I had like to have D006-4376.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is number 17 in your binder. Again taking measures against perpetrators of crimes, the 18th of April. You are reporting that on the 17th of April, persons were arrested and handed over. Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: I sent the military police to arrest those soldiers, but in addition to that, I informed the corps command about what had happened so that they would be aware of what had happened. So that they could be kept abreast of the situation and the unit. Also, I did this so that they could caution other units in Kosovo and Metohija so that such things would not happen elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00701.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when we -- we saw these documents, and at the moment when you handed over these soldiers to the appropriate authorities, did you still command these soldiers, and did you ask about what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No. At the moment when they were handed over to the military prosecutor, of course they were no longer under my authority, and I did not have time to deal with them nor was it my duty. Later on, measures were taken vis-a-vis them by the court, and courts of law are independent. And they acted in accordance with your own jurisdiction. I did not ask any further questions, I didn't have time to deal with them, and I really, to tell you the truth, was not really interested in how they would fare, people who attempted to commit such a crime. That was my position, that if persons committed crimes then they should have appropriate measures taken against them and then may God give them whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now, please, have D011-3280. Before we see this document, I have to say that it's not on our 65 ter list. We did submit this document to our colleagues from the OTP. Or just a second, please -- oh, yes, 701 we have tendered that. So we did mention it in our notice. It's a combat report that was signed by this witness, and if our colleagues from the OTP don't mind, I would like to show this document to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is a regular combat report dated the 21st of April, 1999 that you are sending to the command of the Pristina Corps. In paragraph 1, the one but last sentence says: "The criminals attacked the Maja refugee centre in the Bistrazin village sector where there are no military features or units. They fired 53 (recorded) projectiles. (AB and RZ) of great destructive power completely destroying the entire neighbourhood." Before I ask you for your comment, please look at paragraph 2. The total number of casualties is 6, 32 were wounded, 18 of whom remained in hospital, and one child was critically injured as a result of the enemy attack on the Maja refugee centre. Could you please give us your comment in respect of this report that you've submitted.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. The refugee centre of Maja is near Bistrazin on a farm, a sheep farm. It was Serbs who were staying there, Serbs who had been expelled from the Republic of Serb Krajina during Operation Storm. They were the ones who had been put up in that centre. So it was only Serbs from the Republic of Serb Krajina. They were fired at. It is the air force that hit them, and no one survived the bombing. All the facilities were destroyed as well. There was total destruction. It's not too far away from the Bistrazin bridge. We had a unit of ours that was guarding Bistrazin bridge so that it would not be destroyed. However, that is the area that I'm talking about. That is the area that is referred to in this report. That was the situation there. That was the number of casualties. It was very hard, but basically the centre was levelled to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00702.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask for D006-4383.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 20 in your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we need to turn to that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We have 15 more minutes but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'd like another 15 minutes. For you, you can have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, so that's the exhibit. General, the 23rd of April, 1999. It talks about the contamination of food. I don't really have to read this to you, you can read it for yourself. Please give us your comments regarding this document. It has do with the contamination of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This is a report from my unit sent to the command of the Pristina Corps. Within my unit I had a chief for atomic biological chemical warfare, and he was in charge of detecting any radioactivity. I have to say that after all NATO air-strikes although there was a high risk involved, we did go out to measure where there was increased radioactivity and where there wasn't. Now, what is important here, I'm sending this report on the basis of the findings of this officer of mine. I'm informing the corps command that: "On the 23rd of April, in the area of Osek Hilja village 3 kilometres north of Djakovica, a quantity of flour was found (about 10 tonnes) in the cellar of a house. The flour had been delivered to the inhabitants belonging to the Siptar ethnic minority as part of a humanitarian aid shipment by the Majka Tereza (Mother Theresa humanitarian organisation). The flour was examined using a DRM-3 radiation detector and found to be radioactively contaminated. The radiation measures was 1 to 3 microgrey per hour. It was later established that 3 tonnes had been issued to a bakery, a private bakery to make bread. Steps were taken to stop the production of the bread, and the flour was withdrawn from circulation. The flour is being withdrawn and a pit is being dug at the town garbage dump to bury the flour. The pit is visibly marked using the markings for radioactive sites." And then it is signed by commander Colonel Milos Dosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are at a loss to see its connection with our case, Mr. Popovic. A shipment of flour was from radiation contamination that has come from a humanitarian organisation somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to clarify that with the witness. There are several aspects to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, first and foremost, do you know how it came about that the flour you inspected became contaminated? Secondly, did you undertake all the necessary measures to notify all population that may have used the flour or bakery products containing that flour by the existence of contamination?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Following the request of the Municipal Assembly president to whom certain citizens complained, we sent our chief of the ABHO department to inspect that. That was one of the duties as garrison commander. The municipal president asked that the flour be checked because some people in the town complained of certain problems after having eaten the bread. When we dispatched our chief, he inspected the flour and informed me accordingly. I didn't go there personally, but we had the report of the person who was competent to deal with it fully equipped and experienced. There was no reason to doubt his conclusions. That flour was taken back and deposited at the garbage dump. I can tell you this: The only Siptar working in the town administration was the manager of the public utility company in Djakovica, and he positively knows of the fate of that flour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will not receive the exhibit, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we please have D006-4292.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is your tab 21. We can see that you provided a statement to the commission for co-operation with the ICTY and its expert team. The title is, "Statement on Unit's Activities on the 27th and 28th April, 1999." You have already explained the reasons due to which you provided the previous statement. Did the same reasons apply in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, the very same. The reason was that my statement was sought following the book that was published and following a request made by the commission for co-operation with the ICTY and their expert team. The reason was the same as in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this statement of yours, you mention the 27th and the 28th of March [as interpreted], and participation in the action that took place in the surroundings of Djakovica. In paragraph 1 you say: "By doing so, the Siptar terrorist forces would have created preconditions necessary to receive NATO ground forces should there come time for that. In the aforementioned villages in addition to constant attacks against the MUP and JNA -- and VJ, they also attacked those Albanian citizens who refused to leave those settlements so as to create an image of the Albanian population being forced to leave." Could you please describe the action you referred to here and the area and villages encompassed by it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. The code name of this action was Reka it was an anti-terrorist action in the Caragojsta valley. The closest place to it is Kosare. This was a very important and dangerous stronghold of Siptar terrorists. Should they have been able to achieve successes in Kosare because the land phase of the aggression had already been underway and given that there was lots of combat at Kosare with air support included, should they have been successful there, they could have used a shortest route between Kosare and the valley from which there were roads towards Djakovica, Pec, Klina, et cetera. That was a very important area, in particular, also because it was in the rear of some of our units. On the other hand, by frequent and incessant attacks in this forbidden forested terrain and given that they were in control of all the roads which led to the Kosare border post, they cut off supplies for a number of our units, in a way those units of ours were surrounded. It was for that reason that the corps command and the forward command post decided to neutralise the Siptar terrorist forces in the aforementioned area in order to safe-guard the rear for our units. In that action, smaller parts of my unit took part as well. That is why I was asked to provide this statement to the commission and its expert team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt my learned colleague, but I'm just looking at the transcript page 61, line 11, I believe there's an incorrect date. It says 27th and 28th of March, I believe the document we are looking at concerns the month of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you accept April?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll change what I've noted then.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try to wrap it up and move away from this document. You say that parts of the unit participated in the action. On the next page in both versions you you say: "The officer in command of the unit reported to me that they had no contact with terrorists and that they did not hear or see any activities in the valley of the Trava River." Once you dispatched that unit following the order, who had command over them and who was the officer in charge who conveyed this piece of information to you, and by what means?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: As of the moment when the unit was sent to carry out the task, i.e., to carry out deblocking of the area, they were under the command of the commander in charge of that action. From the brigade, the officer responsible for my part of the unit was Major Zlatko Odak who reported to me that the unit during those two days had no contact with the terrorists and that they did not engage in combat, that no fire was opened upon them, and they -- that no fire was returned. In any case, there was no contact whatsoever with any terrorists. I toured the unit on the 27th, and I saw where their positions were, on the edge of a forest. The area is quite forested, and I fully accept what he told me, that is, that he was unable to see any activities. I believe it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last paragraph of this document says in support of that, that: "After interviews were made with participants of the action and based on my personal insight, I can confirm that neither myself nor any members of my unit participated in any crimes, and I have no knowledge of any other unit committing those." Is this something you can confirm today as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, in full. This is what my officer reported to me and other participants, and I have no other information. This is credible in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll continue discussing this event after the break, and before the break I only seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00703.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To assist counsel in their planning, could we mention that we will try to revert to the former practice of taking the second break in the afternoon at around 5.30 rather than 5.45. We will resume at 18 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is coming, could I mention with respect to Exhibit D609, which was a transcript, that that document will be received under seal as made by counsel at the end of last week, and we will receive a redacted copy as part of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As a separate exhibit to make life easier for the Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the redacted transcript will be Exhibit D609.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go back to P958.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you can follow this on the screen or if it's easier for you, it's 2.7 in your binder. It is your diary. I believe it is at the very beginning of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 37 in B/C/S and 33 in English. I wanted to correct some of the things which appear to be translation mistakes which we noticed when preparing ourselves for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 27th of April, 1999. We see at 8.00, if I'm not mistaken -- did you manage to find it? 2.7 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think it says 8.00. It's a bit difficult to see. It says the action called Reka began in order to clear the terrain of any Siptar terrorist forces, et cetera. The next sentence, could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Action is going according to plan and the tempo is as originally envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And the next sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Because of the absence of the commander (in the 2nd and 4th SAD PVO) and the Chief of Staff of the action, and that is action Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the brackets.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Command organs began their meeting according to plan. Actually, they began working according to plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the English translation that you can see, this sentence in Serbian was translated in a completely different way. General, can you tell us something, the last sentence, it says "Chief of Staff" and then "action Reka," and then there's a completely different part which says "Command organs began working according to plan." Does this have anything to do with action Reka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No, not the last part of that sentence. It merely says that the organs of the command commenced their work at the place where we used to meet every morning, in the command. That meeting was always supposed to be chaired by the commander or the Chief of Staff who also acted as deputy commander. Since we were both absent, I was in the 2nd and 4th Battalion, one was in Pristina and the other one in Gnjilane and the Chief of Staff was absent because he participated in action Reka, those from the command continued work without us. They carried out their activities irrespective of our absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe this clears up the mistake made in the transcript on page -- in the translation on page 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just wonder for the clarity of the record if we shouldn't have the witness read the whole entry out because we've been receiving portions of it. I don't know if it's clear for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please, if that could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please read out the whole paragraph and do not forget mentioning any brackets so as to make everything clear.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a bit illegible. It says: "The Reka clean-up operation of the Siptar terrorists forces began with the participation of the 1st SARD PVO MUB, 1st Rifle Platoon from the command company, and" -- now I can't see very well -- "the 2nd Rifle Platoon of the command battalion. The action is going according to plan as well as the tempo. Due to the absence of the commander (in the 2nd and 4th SARD PVO) and the Chief of Staff (action Reka) meaning he took part in action Reka, the command organs continued their work according to plan. That is to say they continued with their daily briefings as scheduled otherwise."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that is clear now. General, at 11.00 it says: "The brigade commander at the Pristina Corps Command attended an award ceremony of the Order of Gallantry." Is that correct, were you indeed there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. On that day at 11.00 I was at the Pristina Corps Command to attend an award ceremony when the Order of Gallantry decorations were handed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On the screen we can see Exhibit D006-4391. I would ask the usher to help Mr. Dosan mark something on the map that we shall see.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 22, General. And you will soon see it on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, the number is 4291. But I think that's the map. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, maybe it is easier for you to look at the screen, it's easier to see.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, but can we blow it up a bit more? Can we zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to mark on the screen with your pen the position which a part of your unit held during the Reka action.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Let me just see where it was, but this was the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please mark it with number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what was the name of the area where your unit was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: That was the poultry farm because there was a poultry farm here, and this is the area on the Cabrat hill where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So it was all called Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, Cabrat is a big hill which is along the road, but its highest point is above the town of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you make a tour of your units on that position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did make such a tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us once again who was commanding the part of your brigade which was blocking off the area during the Reka action?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: The forces from my brigade were commanded by Major Zlatko Odak.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the Chief of Staff participate in this action as we could see that recorded in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of Staff was also involved but only in his capacity as a commanding officer who could assist Major Odak if he received such orders from those who commanded in it. So he was not commanding the action, he only participated in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was the commander of the whole action, or did you have any influence on the activities of your units during this action?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: No. The action was commanded by the command of the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, or specifically, Colonel Milan Kotor on behalf of the Pristina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what sort of report did you receive once your unit returned? What did the commander who represented your unit in the action have to report to you about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, a subordinate always has to report about a task that was carried out, so once he returned when the task was completed, he reported to me how it was, whether they had carried out the task, whether there had been any problems, any losses, whether they attacked, how much ammunition they had used, and everything else that is normal in a report, so that I could picture how this task, which I received from my Superior Command, had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you directly tell us what was the report like considering all the elements which you just mentioned? What did Major Odak tell you once he returned from the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: The report related to my unit. It said that the task had been carried out, that they did not attack anyone, that no significant incidents occurred, and that the unit returned in good time and that there was nothing that needed any special explanation. The unit had returned in the same composition in which it had left without any problems and without any expenditure of materiel or any losses of manpower. No one was wounded. There was no contact with terrorists, and, therefore, there were no special observations to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please tell us, I'm not sure if this map is the best for this purpose, but you told us about the Siptar terrorist forces which were attacking along the Caragojsta valley from the Republic of Albania, and the specific way in which they used the valley. Can we see it on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: If we were looking at this map, it would be from this direction, because the border is there, and this was the direction from which the Siptar terrorists attacked. If there would be a break-through at Kosare of any specific force, they would come together here and the valley was very favourable for them and therefore it was of great importance for the terrorists. And this is the shortest route.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the directions which you marked with number 2, and please tell us about the route.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: From here roads continue on to Prizren, Pec, and through Rakovina in the direction of Pristina, so this was the most favourable location at which the terrorists could threaten our forces. And where they could launch their activities because if they started from that location as the roads branch into three directions, it would be very difficult to stop them. If these terrorist forces managed to make a major break-through at Kosare. This was the reason why the command had planned this action in order to secure its rear. On the other hand, from this axis here, it's a wooded area. Supply routes for our units at Kosare were constantly in danger, and therefore, the survival of our units up there was threatened. That was the reason why this whole action was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the supply routes and mark them with number 3.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: These are the same routes, I can write the number here, but these are the same routes which are marked as possible routes of -- along which the terrorist could advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I propose to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help me. Is this part of the diary, or is this a separate map?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll ask the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, is this a separate document, or was it a part of the war diary, and are you familiar with this document at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This map is a graphic section which was attached to my statement, which I wrote to the commission for co-operation with ICTY. So it is, in a way, an integral part of my statement which I just read a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The plan will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00704.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see Exhibit D006-4297.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 23 in your binder, General. And before it comes up on the screen, please tell me what was the ethnic composition of your brigade during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, and I remember quite a lot, if I start with the brigade command, my assistant, the assistant for logistics was Lieutenant-Colonel Aleksandar Angelovski, a Macedonian by ethnicity. The assistant for morale and information was Major Zdravko Vinter, a Slovenian. The chief of the security organ was from Djakovica by birth but Slovenian by origin. The chief of the communications at the brigade command was Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Ilic. He was a Croat. The officer at the staff was Captain 1st Class Nike Peraj, he was an Albanian, a Siptar. The desk officer, that is to say the typist at the office was Mrs. Bilajuzare Berisa, Albanian or Siptar by ethnicity. That was the brigade command. In artillery battalions, in the 1st Artillery Battalion, the commander was Lieutenant-Colonel Sabo, Josip, a Hungarian. His deputy was Major Josko Ugljesevic, a Croat. The commander of the command artillery battalion was Velimir Maricic, a Croat. In the logistics battalion, the commander was Ramiz Pejcinovic. He was 1st deputy commander. Later on he became the commander during the war. Ramiz Pejcinovic, he was a Muslim. So these were the officers. As for the non-commissioned officers, they were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the screen we can see a document dated the 6th of April, 1999. It is your tab 23. Under item 5, it says: "Captain 1st Class Nike Peraj will check the level of preparation of the guards between 1100 and 1200 hours in front of the brigade headquarters. He will personally report to me whether the guards have been properly prepared for the execution of their task." Did captain Nike Peraj, was he a member of your unit and what were his duties?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Captain Nike Peraj was a member of my unit. He was at the staff. He is called the third desk officer at the staff which coincided with his rank, and he held the rank of captain 1st class, and his duty was to control, to inspect whether the guards were well prepared and how the change of guard was carried out at the barracks. That was in the town of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00705.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit P313. That is tab 25 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, captain Nike Peraj testified before this court and he has given a number of statements, and this is the last one which I will try to present to you because there are many things concerning your part of the work. You are mentioned in many paragraphs of this statement, and I will ask you to be as brief as possible in your comments because there's lot of material here. First of all, let us please move on to the next page of this document, and if you can please have a look at paragraph 6, which says: "Colonel Milos Dosan was the commander of the 52nd ARBR. He was responsible for the VJ units in the municipality of Djakovica. Colonel Milos Dosan was also responsible for MUP, reservists units," -- and then it says -- "the VJ Corps headquarters received orders from the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade." Can you just briefly comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: In this paragraph, I would say that the only correct statement is the first sentence that I was the commander of the 52nd ARBR of the anti-aircraft defence. Everything else is either partly correct or completely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at the next page and paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says in the territory of the municipality of Djakovica, Prizren, and Pec, there were between 13 and 14.000 soldiers and policemen were deployed there. I heard from colleagues that during the war 150 policemen were deployed there. Your brief comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: That's not true. Quite simply, there weren't that many troops. After all, he could not find out which forces were involved. He could perhaps know how many soldiers our brigade had. That was the only knowledge he could have had. As for the rest, he could not have had that knowledge. It is obvious that there could not have been that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at paragraph 20 now, please, that's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 20, he refers to many volunteers, most of them from Russia, he says, and it says: "We took their details and sent them to the -- we registered them and they were sent to the front at Kosare after the commander Milos Dosan refused their request to stay in Djakovica saying he would not allow them to loot. They were paid by the Territorial Defence of the municipality from where they had come, and the Ministry of Defence in turn funded the Territorial Defence units." Could you please give us your comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: First of all, that is not correct. It is not true that those nine Russians were there, and what is particularly not true is that I received them or that I sent them to the Kosare front. None of this is correct. The only thing that is correct is that we really did have one volunteer who was a physician and who worked in our garrison clinic. He was a Russian. That was the only Russian volunteer that we had. He was a physician, a doctor, at the garrison clinic, and he did his job. All the rest is not true. I did not see them. I did not send them. I did not talk to them about anything, looting or whatever. I never allowed looting, but what he is saying in this specific case is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Paragraph 21, says: "Micunovic also attending meetings with Dosan, under whose command he was, and also Momcilo Stanojevic, also members of the Frenki's units were at one time VJ reservists under Micunovic before joining Frenki's men." Could you please tell what your comments are in this regard so that the Trial Chamber will be clear on what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This statement is completely inaccurate and unprofessional. First of all, Micunovic was not my subordinate officer and therefore he could not attend meetings in my office. He was -- Micunovic was subordinate to the commander of the Pec military department. I did not see him with the mayor of Djakovica. As for Frenki's men. I have no idea about this. No idea whatsoever. I know nothing about that. I did not see them, I did not know who Frenki's men are. I don't find this clear at all, what he is trying to say by this, but it is obvious that he has no idea. This is a pure lie. It is totally removed from the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Paragraph 23 now, the RS Brigade is referred to here, and it says that the VRS Brigade from Republika Srpska was deployed in Rezina. That unit arrived in Djakovica towards the end of February. They had T-55 tanks and anti-aircraft artillery. Could you please give us your comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This is totally meaningless. There was no possibility for anyone to come from Republika Srpska. Secondly, Rezina, the locality of Rezina is in elevation above Djakovica, totally bare, and if so many tanks were to be deployed there, they couldn't move about, and also what sane person would deploy tanks in that kind of area? None of this is true. It is a well-known fact that coming from Republika Srpska -- and it's also a question of whether Republika Srpska had that many tanks and this kind of a brigade. So this is totally illogical and unprofessional.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, General, but there are so many things I'd like to show you in this statement so that's why I'm rushing you through it. Paragraph 25 pertains to the same soldiers from Republika Srpska, and it says: "Their uniforms and equipment were the same as the VJs but with different insignia. My unit provided logistic support to them. I personally saw members of the brigade from the RS having meetings in Dosan's office." Just your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Of course, this is totally untrue. I have nothing to add to that. It is totally untrue. The brigade was not there and therefore, there weren't any meetings, and we did not provide logistics, et cetera. I held meetings with no one in my office from the 24th of March onwards. This is totally senseless. I don't know how to explain this. He used to work at the armoured brigade in Pristina where there were tanks indeed, and I'm so surprised to see him speaking with a total lack of knowledge of -- regarding this matter. And I'm surprised that he even became captain 1st class when he was in his 50s. He just lied so much or he is simply so ignorant, I'm really disappointed by this statement of his. How can he say this possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 28, please. Could you have a look at it. It says: "With regard to collecting all information and reports from different commanders in the field of Djakovica, it was Colonel Branko Kotur from the VJ headquarters was in charge. Kotur would pass the information on to VJ General Colonel Dusan Samardzic, commander of the VJ headquarters in Nis." Please give us your comment.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: In this sentence there's so many lies that is unbelievable. First of all, there is no Branko Kotur. There is Colonel Milan Kotur, who was not in that line of work at all. He was an infantry man. He did not collect any kind of information. Secondly, it says: "The staff or headquarters of the VJ Corps" -- then he says "to the VJ headquarters in Nis, Dusan Samardzic." Dusan Samardzic was not army commander at the time, it was General Pavkovic who was army commander at the time, so it is not customary at all for lower-ranking officers to submit reports to their 2nd Superior Command so this is totally incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. For the transcript, I think that you said that there are so many lies here that it is unbelievable. There is a negation in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: There are so many lies here that it is unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please have a look at paragraph 37. Nikola Micunovic, also known as Dragan, was chief of the Vojni Odsjek in Djakovica, but he just had an administrative role in peacetime concerning Territorial Defence. In war time, he was operational commander of the Territorial Defence for the Djakovica municipalities. Micunovic reported to Dosan and to mayor Stanojevic. Again, your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, yet again, the same thing. In Djakovica there was no Vojni Odsjek or military department. Djakovica did not have a Vojni Odsjek, and he was not its head. For a while he was head of the military territorial detachment, and he was subordinated to the commander of the Vojni Odsjek or military department in Pec. He was not subordinated to me, and he certainly could not have been subordinated to the mayor, the president of the municipality. Quite simply military units cannot be subordinated to civilians in that level. So this is totally incorrect. It's a lie quite simply. It's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please have a look at paragraph 43 now, the last sentence: "I was once sent by Dosan to put a stop to the drinking but with the drunken state of the people in the hotel and their weaponry, it would have been too risky, so it was not pursued."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off, we can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not true. I did not allow people to drink, but people were not drunk because there was no liquor being served at the hotel there. However, even if that had been the case, I wouldn't have sent him. It would not have been right for me to send him as an Albanian to expose him to danger, for that reason. So none of this is correct. The only thing that is correct is that I consistently forbade drinking and, therefore, intoxication.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 47, please. Again the last sentence: "I drove the ARBR commander a few times to meetings between the MUP and the VJ. These meetings occurred at various locations: MUP headquarters, VJ headquarters, or the municipality building always in the basement for safety." Again your brief comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, he never drove me. I had two drivers of my own who took turns at driving me. There was no logic for a captain 1st class to drive a Colonel. So that's not correct. He did not drive me to meetings. I said that meetings were held from time to time but already at this stage of the war there were less and less of them. Quite simply, for them to be held at the MUP headquarters or VJ headquarters, that is not true. So this statement of his is not correct. He did not drive me and even when meetings were being held, they were not held at these locations?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please look at paragraph 50. It says: "Once Dosan called me from a meeting and said that the unit near Ljug Bunar, north-east of Djakovica should be moved to Kosare. I then had to pass this information on to the operation staff of the ARBR major Zdravko Vinter. This unit was part of Dosan's ARBR." Again a brief comment, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: This is not true. That is not the usual way things are done. As a matter of fact for security reasons, such orders were never given over the telephone where -- which unit would go. I especially would not give that order to him. I would give the order to the commander of the unit that was supposed to go. That is customary procedure. I commanded the commanders, and they received orders from me, otherwise information twice or thrice removed as would be the case here, that is not possible. Zdravko Vinter was not operations chief. He was my assistant commander for morale, and he could not issue any orders to any commander on my behalf. This would be a total violation of subordination. It would disrupt the chain of command and therefore this is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, 51, he says: "Once after a meeting I had to separate Dosan and Micunovic because they were arguing. I do not know what they were fighting over. On the same occasion, Dosan got into the car with me, he said that Kovacevic and Micunovic were doing unauthorised things and blaming it on the VJ. Micunovic's VJ reserve unit had killed eight civilians in Deva village at the end of March 1999." First of all, was Micunovic's unit from the VJ reserve? And could I hear your comment with regard to all of this that he is saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN
utterances.text: Micunovic's unit was the Territorial Defence unit that had its own tasks and its own chain of command like any other unit. Other the other hand, there is no truth whatsoever in this. I mean, why would I argue with Micunovic? Why would I as garrison commander and a colonel argue with him, and why would he separate us? I'm not that kind of person, and this is not the way people behave in the army and in view of subordination and everything. And also over here where he says that Micunovic was doing unauthorised things and Kovacevic, had I known that they were doing something unauthorised or impermissible, I would inform my commander about that. I would not discuss it with my subordinate. That is not the right way to behalf. It is not customary either. It is not the right thing to do from the point of view of morality as well, and that is not the way an army functions either. It's not true. Quite simply -- I mean, I'm tempted to say that he simply did not know what he was saying when he was saying all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a few more paragraphs that I would like to show to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That can't be done tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's why we should leave it for tomorrow because our time is up, and tomorrow I will make an effort to bring the direct examination to end as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We now adjourn and resume at 2.15 tomorrow.
